schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Strength Peaks at 20-28 and Declines About 1% a Year After 30: Lab and Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes

**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
declines by approximately 1% per year (PDF p. 170, printed p. 159). The text compares two
measurement approaches: laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al
1961; MacDougall et al 1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across
juvenile, junior, senior, and Masters (over 40) age-group records (Table 3.6, PDF p. 171,
printed p. 160). The two datasets correspond reasonably well through adolescence but
diverge outside that range: below about age 14, lifting percentages run *higher* than lab
percentages (at age 10: lab 42%, lifting 59%), which the text attributes to weight-trained
children being much stronger than their untrained peers; over about 45 years, lifting
percentages fall *below* lab percentages (at age 65: lab 74%, lifting 49%), which the text
attributes to Olympic weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across
many muscle groups, versus dynamometer testing of one limited muscle group (usually the
quadriceps). Linear regression fits the 30-80 age decline separately for each dataset: for
untrained lab subjects, %S = 120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S =
140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996), where A is age in years and %S is the percentage of one's own
peak strength (eqs 3.8-3.9, printed 160). The trained-lifter curve declines about twice as
fast, in percentage-of-peak terms, as the untrained-lab curve, and neither coefficient
matches the "approximately 1% per annum" the same section states earlier (printed 159).
Record all three figures as given: the text does not reconcile them, and this entry does
not harmonize them either. (PDF pp. 170-171, printed pp. 159-160, "3.3.7 The Relationship
between Strength and Age," Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline itself.
**Inference:** this is broadly consistent with ordinary age-related neuromuscular decline,
though the text gives no citation for that and none is supplied here. For *why the two
measurement methods disagree* at the extremes, the text gives a stated reason at each end,
not a single unifying mechanism: below about 14, weight-trained children are simply much
stronger than untrained same-age peers, which biases the comparison at that end; over 45,
Olympic weightlifting's agility and strength-speed demands across many muscle groups pull
lifting scores below dynamometer scores at that end (printed 160). The authors do not
frame this as skill "masking" the older lifters' true underlying strength; they present
lab and lifting as two different measurements of different things, not one measurement
that is closer to the truth than the other.

**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer or force-plate
testing may better isolate raw strength for very young or very old populations, while
competition-style multi-joint lift performance folds in accumulated technical skill and,
at the older end, a different demand structure (agility, strength-speed) than raw strength
alone. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen through fifth-year
seniors, and any over-45 staff testing), raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift differs systematically by
experience or class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
underlying strength. This reasoning is rebuilt from the corrected direction of the
lab-versus-lifting disagreement above; an earlier draft of this entry had that direction
reversed.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific regression equations are fit to weightlifting records
and a small number of lab studies (Hettinger 1961; MacDougall 1982) predating this text's
publication; the exact numeric coefficients (120.17, 0.68865, 140.15, 1.3853) should be
treated as illustrative of that era's data and that specific population, not as a precise,
individually-applicable age-adjustment formula for a current athlete population. This entry
does not claim the underlying decline pattern is independently confirmed beyond these
cited sources; no other source is named here to corroborate it.

**Example** — The book's own worked example (not invented here): a young lifter weighing
90 kg with a 350 kg Olympic total is bodymass-adjusted to 86.3% (no age adjustment needed).
A 45-year-old lifter weighing 80 kg with a 260 kg total is bodymass-adjusted to 67.8%; the
age adjustment for 45 years (%S = 77.8%) is then divided into that score to give a final
87.1%. So the older lifter, despite the smaller raw total, has the higher combined
relative-strength score (PDF p. 171, printed p. 160).

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the paired bodymass-adjustment
method this age adjustment is explicitly combined with).

# Strength Peaks at 20-28 and Declines About 1% a Year After 30: Lab and Competition Data Disagree at the Extremes

**What it is** — Strength peaks between roughly ages 20-28 for both men and women, then
declines by approximately 1% per year (PDF p. 170, printed p. 159). The text compares two
measurement approaches: laboratory isometric/isokinetic dynamometer data (Hettinger et al
1961; MacDougall et al 1982) versus real weightlifting competition performance across
juvenile, junior, senior, and Masters (over 40) age-group records (Table 3.6, PDF p. 171,
printed p. 160). The two datasets correspond reasonably well through adolescence but
diverge outside that range: below about age 14, lifting percentages run *higher* than lab
percentages (at age 10: lab 42%, lifting 59%), which the text attributes to weight-trained
children being much stronger than their untrained peers; over about 45 years, lifting
percentages fall *below* lab percentages (at age 65: lab 74%, lifting 49%), which the text
attributes to Olympic weightlifting's added demand for agility and strength-speed across
many muscle groups, versus dynamometer testing of one limited muscle group (usually the
quadriceps). Linear regression fits the 30-80 age decline separately for each dataset: for
untrained lab subjects, %S = 120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S =
140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996), where A is age in years and %S is the percentage of one's own
peak strength (eqs 3.8-3.9, printed 160). The trained-lifter curve declines about twice as
fast, in percentage-of-peak terms, as the untrained-lab curve, and neither coefficient
matches the "approximately 1% per annum" the same section states earlier (printed 159).
Record all three figures as given: the text does not reconcile them, and this entry does
not harmonize them either. (PDF pp. 170-171, printed pp. 159-160, "3.3.7 The Relationship
between Strength and Age," Table 3.6, Fig 3.25.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the underlying age-strength decline itself.
**Inference:** this is broadly consistent with ordinary age-related neuromuscular decline,
though the text gives no citation for that and none is supplied here. For *why the two
measurement methods disagree* at the extremes, the text gives a stated reason at each end,
not a single unifying mechanism: below about 14, weight-trained children are simply much
stronger than untrained same-age peers, which biases the comparison at that end; over 45,
Olympic weightlifting's agility and strength-speed demands across many muscle groups pull
lifting scores below dynamometer scores at that end (printed 160). The authors do not
frame this as skill "masking" the older lifters' true underlying strength; they present
lab and lifting as two different measurements of different things, not one measurement
that is closer to the truth than the other.

**When to apply** — Use the disagreement-at-the-extremes finding to choose the right
measurement approach for the population in question: isolated dynamometer or force-plate
testing may better isolate raw strength for very young or very old populations, while
competition-style multi-joint lift performance folds in accumulated technical skill and,
at the older end, a different demand structure (agility, strength-speed) than raw strength
alone. **Inference:** for Baylor's mixed-age roster (true freshmen through fifth-year
seniors, and any over-45 staff testing), raw 1RM comparisons across class years should be
read cautiously if technical proficiency in the tested lift differs systematically by
experience or class year, since that skill difference can move the number independent of
underlying strength. This reasoning is rebuilt from the corrected direction of the
lab-versus-lifting disagreement above; an earlier draft of this entry had that direction
reversed.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific regression equations are fit to weightlifting records
and a small number of lab studies (Hettinger 1961; MacDougall 1982) predating this text's
publication; the exact numeric coefficients (120.17, 0.68865, 140.15, 1.3853) should be
treated as illustrative of that era's data and that specific population, not as a precise,
individually-applicable age-adjustment formula for a current athlete population. This entry
does not claim the underlying decline pattern is independently confirmed beyond these
cited sources; no other source is named here to corroborate it.

**Example** — The book's own worked example (not invented here): a young lifter weighing
90 kg with a 350 kg Olympic total is bodymass-adjusted to 86.3% (no age adjustment needed).
A 45-year-old lifter weighing 80 kg with a 260 kg total is bodymass-adjusted to 67.8%; the
age adjustment for 45 years (%S = 77.8%) is then divided into that score to give a final
87.1%. So the older lifter, despite the smaller raw total, has the higher combined
relative-strength score (PDF p. 171, printed p. 160).

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the paired bodymass-adjustment
method this age adjustment is explicitly combined with).

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; the authors report that Siff and mechanical-engineering students at the
University of the Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under
non-isokinetic dynamic conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the
resulting dynamic force-angle curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves
obtained statically. The curve profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and
joint orientation: for example, maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance)
elbow flexion does not occur near 90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full
flexion, and evoking the myotatic stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension
produces yet another profile. The same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves
versus curves measured under unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in
the chapter, the authors state directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are
unable to measure functional maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive
strength," so it is "futile" to use them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on
sporting preparedness or progress (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed
p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15). This "futile" statement sits against the book's own
practice elsewhere: it computes explosive strength (Se) from isometric tension, "0.5 Fmax
over its time" (printed 102, 108); calls starting strength "always produced under
conditions of isometric muscle action" and says that fact "dispels the opinion that ...
isometric training should be completely abandoned" (printed 109); and builds the
functional/polyfunctional profile in part from "explosive-isometric muscular tension"
(printed 111-112, see
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). The text
does not reconcile the "futile" statement with these uses; this entry does not resolve it
either.

**Why it works** — The authors' own stated reason, given for the force-angle curve
specifically, is that curves are "determined by the type of muscle contraction, the
velocity of movement, the starting conditions, the load and the orientation of the joint"
(printed 103). **Inference:** a broader mechanism (not stated in the text) is that
isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular velocity, removing
the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage and release, and multi-joint coordination
that dynamic sporting movements actually use.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the isometric seated calf raise is run on the
ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed 90-degree ankle/knee position
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested**: this entry sits against the book's own
internal contradiction described above (the "futile" statement versus the book's own
isometric-derived explosive-strength, starting-strength, and functional-profile measures),
and against vault evidence of a moderate real relationship. Thomas et al 2015 (vault,
`research-papers/thomas-2015-...`) found isometric mid-thigh pull (IMTP) impulse correlates
with countermovement-jump and squat-jump peak force and power (r = 0.49-0.64), though not
with jump height. **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has no
value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance."
The caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests, alone, to infer
dynamic, functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all; the entry's
`contested` rating reflects that the book itself does not consistently follow its own
caution.

**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak measured at the wrong joint angle for the sport
skill can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive performance. The device itself cannot
measure rate of force development or explosive strength directly, per the authors' own
"futile" statement above, so a slow-RFD finding from an isometric test should not be cited
as evidence of that device's own output.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

21	of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
22	**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
23	reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
24	rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
25	physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
26	factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
27	irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
28	system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
29	variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
30	mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
31	pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
32	repetitive contributions. Relative to the body, the strength field also consists of two
33	systems: the *external interaction* with the motor apparatus, and the *internal
34	interaction* with the motor apparatus. The two appear simultaneously and act somewhat
35	independently, but influence each other increasingly as sports proficiency improves; control
36	of the external interaction "is possible only through the internal kinesiological pattern"
37	(printed 107). (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — The authors define the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. Relative to the body, the strength field also consists of two
systems: the *external interaction* with the motor apparatus, and the *internal
interaction* with the motor apparatus. The two appear simultaneously and act somewhat
independently, but influence each other increasingly as sports proficiency improves; control
of the external interaction "is possible only through the internal kinesiological pattern"
(printed 107). (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component; the text itself only
says each component "must be considered when ... selecting the special strength-training
means" (printed 107) without naming which method targets which component. **Inference:** a
movement that depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) plausibly calls for
plyometric or reactive methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force
(component 1) plausibly calls for more conventional strength methods; this mapping is not
stated in the text. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active
quadriceps/glute drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy
stored during the countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being
redirected (component 4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak
amortization phase is likely under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused
(component 1) training emphasis would not fix. This example and interpretation are not in
the source.

[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1),
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] (Chapter 1).

# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once

**What it is** — The authors term "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (Verkhoshansky's coinage for the phenomenon,
1977). Two forms are described. (1) **Strength-quality order**: maximum/absolute strength
(So, confined in this text's own usage to maximum involuntary strength, see printed 107)
increases from the start of training; explosive strength (Se) begins increasing next, later;
starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the introduction of
near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**: which muscle group
carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole vaulting, the abdominal
muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the shoulder flexors take
over that functional role as mastery grows while elbow-extensor strength rises uniformly
over the same period (Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation
between athletic result and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite),
while the correlation with leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite)
(Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related sequence is given for starting-strength in jumpers and
sprinters: ankle flexion develops first (bearing the earliest, most intense load), then hip
extension (grouped with knee extension in the text's discussion), and finally hip flexion,
developing later and less intensely (hip flexors only oppose gravity and one limb's inertia,
a smaller demand). The text separately notes that the approximately linear rise of maximum
and absolute strength described above is typical only of sports where the athlete overcomes
relatively small resistance and the speed of producing force matters more than its
magnitude (printed 114); this caveat attaches to that linear-rise finding specifically, not
to the three-quality development order as a whole. (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115,
Figs 2.21-2.22.)

**Why it works** — For the strength-quality order, the authors attribute the pattern to
which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized,
near-competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest
in a periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, they attribute it to which muscle groups
bear the largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are
loaded most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much
less so, since they only move a single limb against gravity).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** use the strength-quality order (absolute, then explosive,
then starting-strength) as a rough sequencing guide within a periodized plan, consistent with
the classic strength-to-power progression already in Eric's baseline: **Eric's baseline:**
off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first, with
already-strong athletes shifting more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). **Inference:** this claim adds a further,
specific step this baseline does not name: starting-strength (the ability to build force
fastest right at the onset of contraction) is described here as the *last* quality to develop
significantly, tied specifically to near-competition-intensity sport-specific work rather
than general strength or speed-strength training; a plan that stops at speed-strength work
may be leaving starting-strength underdeveloped without adding sport-specific,
near-competition-intensity exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from a small number of Soviet single-sport case studies
(pole vault, shot put, plus unnamed jumpers/sprinters), not a broad multi-sport sample;
**Inference:** do not assume the exact muscle-group sequence (ankle flexion, then hip
extension, then hip flexion) generalizes unchanged to football-specific skills, which load
the ankle and hip in different relative proportions than pole vaulting or shot put. The
approximately linear rise of maximum and absolute strength is stated to hold mainly for
"sports where the athlete overcomes relatively small resistance, and where the speed of
producing working force ... is most important" (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114), which does not
obviously describe heavy-resistance line-play skills; this caveat is about that linear-rise
finding, not the three-quality order as a whole.

**Example** — **Inference:** a freshman football player early in a strength program would
be expected, per this claim, to show his fastest early gains in general/absolute strength;
explosive-strength gains (jump, throw-type output) should follow once absolute strength is
established; and the sharpest gains in true starting-strength (a fast first movement) should
be expected latest, once near-game-intensity technical and speed work is added, not from
weight-room strength work alone. This example, including the equation of starting-strength
with "get-off at the snap," is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (Chapter 1, the
biochemical-level version of the same named phenomenon),
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]].

92	## Conditioning and energy systems
93

96	- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
97	- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
98	- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]

100	- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]

157	- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
158	- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
159	- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]
160	- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]
161	
162	## Education and staff development
163	
164	- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
165	- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]
166	- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
167	- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]
168	
169	---
170	
171	## No material found
172	
173	None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.
174	
175	---
176	
177	## Tensions and contradictions
178	
179	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
180	
181	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
182	
183	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
184	
185	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
186	
187	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
188	
189	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
190	
191	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
192	
193	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
194	
195	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
196	
197	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.
198	
199	---
200	
201	## Named influences
202	
203	| Influence | What's credited to them | Where | Provenance |
204	|---|---|---|---|
205	| Al Vermeil (transcribed once as "Albert Meal") | Hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity → strength → power → speed → sport skill); described as the department's programming "compass" | class1-transcript.md pp.9-10, 18-19 | Course material, speaker unconfirmed |
206	| Dan Pfaff (transcribed as "Coach Path/Paf/Pabst") | The "coach's eye" ideal — biomechanical assessment purely by trained observation, illustrated with an anecdote about diagnosing a runner's spinal alignment from 50 meters away | class1-transcript.md pp.6-7 | Course material, speaker unconfirmed |
207	| Yuri Verkhoshansky | Principle of Dynamic Correspondence, for judging real exercise transfer | class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34 | Course material |
208	| Anatoly Bondarchuk (transcribed as "Bondurciu") | General prep / specific prep / specific development / competitive exercise taxonomy | class1-transcript.md p.16; week1-lecture.md p.36 | Course material |
209	| Johnny Parker, Al Miller, Rob Panariello (transcribed as "Panarillo") | Undulating/non-linear periodization model, described as personally preferred | class1-transcript.md pp.25-26; week1-lecture.md pp.59-63; lesson8summary.md #19 | Course material |
210	| Louis Simmons / Westside Barbell (via Zatsiorsky and Siff) | Conjugate/concurrent method: max effort, dynamic effort, repetitive effort | class1-transcript.md pp.26-27; week1-lecture.md pp.63-66 | Course material |
211	| A.S. Prilepin (transcribed once as "the Philippines chart") | Rep/set/intensity guide, used as the default across strength and power teaching | class1-transcript.md p.19; week1-lecture.md p.47; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15 | Shared team material |
212	| Tracy Fober | "Use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" — quality-first coaching maxim, cited from a 2019 Baylor AP clinic and her Instagram | class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46 | Course material |
213	| Stu McMillan | Four goals of strength training (produce force, absorb force, decrease injury chance, teach positional context) | lesson8summary.md #3; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.5 | Wenger's session (Mar. 19) |
214	| Fred Hatfield; JL Holdsworth | Strength/alignment aphorisms ("can't shoot a cannon out of a canoe"; "monster tires on a Prius with bad alignment") | hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.4; lesson8summary.md #2 | Wenger's session |
215	| Joel Jamieson (*Ultimate MMA Conditioning*) | Recommended as the best practical resource on energy-system development methods | 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12; week3-lecture.md pp.49-50 | Eric's assigned session (transcript speaker unconfirmed; slides confirmed) |
216	| Jason Avedesian / Clemson Olympic Sports Science | Entire intern curriculum (force plates, GPS, force-velocity profiling, data hygiene, visualization, soft skills, research methods, injury risk, S&C) | intencurriculumn.md, all pages | Reference source, not Eric's voice — used by the Development Plan as a benchmark |
217	| Hawkin Dynamics | Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) metric-selection framework for force-plate reporting | hd-odsf-metrics.md | Vendor framework, adopted as practice |
